name: Warm Springs Sahaptin
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.

(Open PDF:https://journals.uvic.ca/index.php/WPLC/article/download/5512/2119.) Supporting general-Sahaptin statement: Rude, Noel. 2006. Proto-Sahaptian vocalism. Papers for ICSNL 41 (UBCWPL 18): 264-277, p. 272; Rude, Noel. 2012. Reconstructing Proto-Sahaptian sounds. Papers for ICSNL 47 (UBCWPL 32): 292-324, p. 302.
catalog_locator: Hymes 1984 p. 235, first paragraph (of the 4-page landscape scan; p. 235 occupies the left half of that page); cf. p. 229 opening paragraph and p. 234 last paragraph.
catalog_quote: The other difference lies in the fact that there are a large number of words in Warm Springs Sahaptin in which a stressed vowel that occurs in that word in the other dialects is not present and the stress has been shifted to the other vowel of the word. These missing vowels may be either obscure stressed vowels (which Jacobs says never drop out in the Northwest dialects in the way that unstressed vowels may) or full vowels. A few examples out of the many I have collected are:(WS forms first) pt'x̣ánu 'wooded mountain' vs. pə́t'x̣anu; twít'aš 'grizzly bear' vs. túwit'aš; ápx 'hide,skin' vs. əpə́x; núkʷt 'meat' vs. nəkʷə́t. In future, I hope to be able to document this process more fully. Its interest lies, it seems to me, in the suggestion it gives that Sahaptin is a language in which the consonants are somehow more important to the identity of the lexeme than the vowels. If one sees how vowels may be lost, stress may shift and yet the consonantal skeleton of the word remains one is prompted to think of another feature of all Sahaptin dialects ...

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tenino/Warm Springs is a Sahaptin dialect: each word carries one primary stress (realised as high pitch), and its position is a lexical property of the morphemes, not derived from syllable count or weight (Rude 2006:272, 2012:302-304; Jansen 2010:52-57; Hargus & Beavert 2014 sec. 4.1: 'stress is morpheme inherent in Sahaptin', with stressed suffixes outranking prefixes outranking roots). Hymes 1984 is the only Warm-Springs-specific published statement: p. 229 endorses Jacobs' 1931 sketch as 'roughly valid' for Warm Springs, and p. 235 reports that Warm Springs has dropped the historically stressed vowel of many words and moved the stress to the remaining vowel (pt'xánu, twít'aš, ápx, núkʷt), so Warm Springs stress positions differ lexically from Umatilla/Yakima ones. No source gives a Tenino-specific default-position rule.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Hymes 1984 says nothing. Jacobs 1931:117 (snippet): Northwest dialects have 'only one syllable accented and no secondary stress', but 'in the Umatilla reservation dialects there may be two, three or four accented syllables to a word'. Rude 2012:302 claims three stress levels for Sahaptin generally with secondary stress considered 'more or less predictable' (Rude 1988: bisyllabic reduplication k'ùsik'úsi 'dog', imperfective past -shàna, habitual -xàna); Hargus & Beavert 2016 find no secondary stress in Yakima. Nothing reported for Warm Springs.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress is lexically variable across dialects: Jansen 2010:9 notes the stress of shushaynsh 'steelhead' varies by dialect; Morrison 1990 (per Jansen 2010:275) gives Warm Springs nominaliser -ya with stress on the preceding syllable after polysyllabic C-final nouns vs. stressed -yay elsewhere; unaccented function words such as ku 'and' and pronominal clitics never take stress (Jacobs 1931:117; Hargus & Beavert 2014 sec. 4.1).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: one accent per phonological word (clitics attach unstressed); citation forms of nouns and verbs. Hymes' data are from Warm Springs (Tenino/Tygh/Wyam speakers on the Warm Springs reservation), 1970s-80s fieldwork; the general rule comes from Umatilla (Rude) and Yakima (Jansen, Hargus & Beavert) descriptions applied to Sahaptin as a whole.
new_statements.identity_note: Hymes 1984 describes 'Warm Springs Sahaptin', the speech of the Warm Springs reservation (Tenino, Tygh Valley, Wyam/Celilo, John Day speakers), which is what Glottolog teni1238 covers (alt. name 'Warm Springs'; Columbia River Sahaptin cluster with Umatilla umat1237). The general stress rule quoted alongside comes from Umatilla (Rude) and Yakima yaki1237 (Jansen; Hargus & Beavert) data stated for Sahaptin as a whole, not from Tenino data.

new_statements.quote: In adverbs, particles and many nouns that are devoid of affixes, it seems impossible to determine rules for the presence of stress; accident, traditional usage, many unascertainable factors seem to have play. Wherever morphologic affixes are used, stress is governed rigidly by such grammatical factors. Definite rules may be formulated, based on the affixes present. [...] In the verb, stress is largely governed by the pronominal, modal and temporal ideas expressed in the verb. The root is stressed if nothing else is stressed. [...] In most other cases in the verb, stress is on the initial syllable of the verb root complex unless one of the following derivational affixes appear.

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the catalog record (classification lexical, Hymes 1984, rule empty) and the existing statement 'lexical (unpredictable)': Jacobs likewise gives no positional or weight rule and says stress in unaffixed words is unpredictable. He adds the morphological system behind it (inherently accented affixes outrank the root; default verb stress on the initial syllable of the root complex; ranked accented noun postpositions; culminativity with no secondary stress in NW Sahaptin; tonal realization) and the dialect split (Umatilla-reservation walu'la-palu's: several accents per word, penultimate drift). Caveat on identity: Jacobs's data are northwest Sahaptin (Klikitat, upper Cowlitz), which…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress (= high/falling tone on the stressed syllable) is not fixed by position or weight. In words without affixes (adverbs, particles, many nouns) its place cannot be predicted and must be learned per word. In affixed words it is fixed by the morphology: certain affixes are inherently accented and always take the word stress (verb prefixes a'- 3rd person and pa'-; verb suffixes -i'k, -a't, -a'c, -pama', -a'taD; a list of accented prefixes/anterior roots p. 119; noun postpositional suffixes -pama', -Gwa'k, -i'k, -ti'k, -(y)a'i, -(ne)mi', with possessive -mi' outranking -pama' and -pama' outranking the rest, except rare final -aipa'x, -xana'tt); otherwise the verb is stressed on the initial syllable of the root complex ('the root is stressed if nothing else is stressed'); demonstratives/pronouns stress prefixed i'- if present, else the pronoun root (first syllable) unless an accented suffix occurs. p. 117: stressed short vowels carry high tone, stressed long vowels/diphthongs falling tone; every monosyllabic word is stressed. Syllable weight (p. 116-117) affects the tone contour, not the place of stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 117: in northwest Sahaptin 'ordinary words have only one syllable accented and no secondary stress; freshly compounded words may have two equally stressed syllables'; in the Umatilla reservation dialects (walu'la-palu's) 'there may be two, three or four accented syllables to a word, each accent gentle, with only slightly higher tone' (p. 120: each verb root stressed, first and third of three roots, enclitics may be stressed).
new_statements.exceptions: p. 117-118: connective ku- and the pronominal enclitics never take stress; a'uku etc. vary; p. 118: stress alone distinguishes pa'- (me/him; 2>1) from pa- (they): pa'watana '(you) struck at me / hit him' vs pawa'tana 'they struck at' -- 'the only homonyms in the language'; p. 119: anterior root -qala- 'roll' is almost never accented even when root-initial, accent going to the next root element (exceptions p. 170); palu's-only final past -ya' accentuation; walu'la-palu's: aspect/tense suffixes take stress when followed by a suffix or enclitic (-xa'na, -ca'na), and 'one of the essential accentual drifts in the walu'la-palu's verb has been towards the penultimate syllable'; p. 120: adverbs of manner derived from verb roots and duplicated bisyllabic nouns are accented on the second syllable (ku'ci -> kuci'kuci); in NW Sahaptin the only coordinate stresses in non-compounds are iwa'tca' 'he was', pawa'tca' 'they were'.
new_statements.identity_note: Jacobs 1931 is built on two northwest Sahaptin (Cascades) dialects, Klikitat (xwa'lxwaipam, 1926) and upper Cowlitz (ta'iDnapam, 1927), with less complete notes on the Umatilla-reservation provincialisms (yumati'la, walu'la, palu's). Warm Springs (Tenino, John Day etc., 'Warmsprings' in Jacobs) is not directly recorded: p. 96 'The bands now resident on Warmsprings reservation, Oregon, understand and are understood by the other northern Sahaptins; no careful recording of their provincialisms is available, as far as I know; the present sketch should be roughly valid, no doubt, for the Warmsprings bands.' The stress rules quoted are explicitly 'rules for stress in the verb of northwest Sahaptin'. For teni1238 the work is therefore a closely related-dialect description endorsed as approximately valid by both Jacobs and Hymes 1984 (p. 229).

sources.note: Sec. 4.1 Lexical pitch accent: 'Sahaptin morphemes are either underlyingly accented or unaccented'; words surface with one accent; suffix accent wins over root, prefix over root. Yakima/NW data; lists Warm Springs and John Day as Columbia River subdialects.

sources.citation: Rude, Noel. 2012. Reconstructing Proto-Sahaptian sounds. Papers for ICSNL 47 (UBCWPL 32): 292-324.
sources.note: Sec. 2 Stress, pp. 302-304: 'Nez Perce and Sahaptin are syllable timed languages with three levels of stress.. In Sahaptin all lexical morphemes have morpheme inherent stress'; morphemes with inherent stress follow a hierarchy suffix > prefix > root (itxata / patxata / patxatala). Sahaptin data are Umatilla (Columbia River cluster, same cluster as Tenino) with some WS forms; not Tenino-specific.

sources.note: Sec. 2.6 pp. 52-57 (Yakima, NW dialect): one primary stress per word, root stress not predictable, stress-stealing affixes; notes stress of shushaynsh 'steelhead' varies among dialects (p. 9) and that Morrison (1990) Warm Springs Grammar gives -ya with stress on the preceding syllable for polysyllabic C-final nouns (p. 275).
